9e7c7b702041: <0>P-44 (around 1955).</0> The <1>Post</1> assigned "one of its star writers, Jack Alexander" (P-44). He had just written about the New Jersey rackets and came to A.A. expecting little, but "he soon became an A.A. 'convert,' even though he wasn't an alcoholic" (P-44). He spent a whole month with them; Dr. Bob, Bill and the elders of the groups at Akron, New York, Cleveland, Philadelphia and Chicago spent hours with him (P-44). The piece "was the lead story in the Saturday Evening Post of March 1, 1941." (P-44).
0bd1f79cd66f: Then six thousand appeals for help hit the New York office (P-44). Form letters wouldn't do; every one had to have a personal reply, and Bill says, "An enormous Twelfth Step job had to be done and done quickly." (P-44). For the first time the office asked the groups for money, with $1.00 per member per year as the measure, kept in a fund for office work only (P-44). The year began with two thousand members and ended with eight thousand (P-44). Public relations on that scale were new, and the lessons learned, among them anonymity at the public level and "public relations by the principle of attraction rather than promotion," can be seen in the Traditions (P-44).

Hospitals gave A.A. working arrangements, consulted it and employed A.A. nurses, and these relationships worked well, but none of these places were known as A.A. hospitals (P-17, p. 33).
f16cc102b667: <0>The line for groups.</0> "Neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A." (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 24). Groups can't endorse, finance or ally with any other cause, however good, or link A.A.'s name to other alcohol work so that the public thinks A.A. has given up its own aim (P-17, p. 24). Members and friends in those fields should be discouraged from stressing A.A.'s name in publicity or fund-raising (P-17, pp. 24–25).
1186a1f365cf: <0>The freedom for members.</0> Bill calls the "do nothing" view unthinkable (P-17, p. 25). Members can bring their experience to other noncontroversial alcohol work if they act as individuals: no A.A. label in public and no use of A.A. status to raise money (P-17, p. 25). His summary: "A.A. does not sponsor projects in other fields" (P-17, "Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects", 1947, p. 25), but members may work in constructive ones as individuals, careful of A.A.'s name (P-17, pp. 25–26).
b64559aa8a3e: Bill's 1955 foreword asks A.A. to "steadfastly decline all political, sectarian, or other alliances" (P-17, Foreword, 1955, p. 4). f82273ba39e5: It doesn't mean groups can't meet in churches, hospitals or treatment centres (a later pamphlet describes such groups as renting space there; P-16, 2018, pp. 17–18), or that A.A. can't work alongside hospitals and doctors; all of that is cooperation. It doesn't stop individual members working in other fields as individuals, provided they keep A.A.'s name out of it, and it doesn't bind outside organizations.
